newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank economists see moderate growth.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank economists see moderate growth.

text.p: The economy is likely to expand at a moderate rate of around 2 percent in 1997 but slightly stronger-than-expected growth could raise the risk of higher inflation, a group of bank economists said Wednesday.

The Economic Advisory Committee to the American Bankers Association expressed concern about labour shortages in certain areas of the country and said should the situation worsen, wage pressures and inflation could rise.

"Tight labour markets are causing wages to rise in many parts of the country," said Joel Naroff, chairman of the committee. "If growth is any stronger, the ability of productivity to offset wage increases before they trigger higher prices could be impaired."
The panel predicted that inflation would average around 3 percent this year.
However, Naroff said there was uncertainty in the outlook for both growth and inflation and that the direction of prices was a big concern for the panel.
Should the economy grow even slightly faster than the expected 2 percent rate, the Fed might be forced to raise interest rates to head off the inflationary threat, the group predicted.

Such a move was by no means viewed as a certainty, though. The group also saw a possibility that consumer demand, which has helped fuel six years of economic expansion, could begin to taper off, causing the economy to turn sluggish.
If that were to occur, the Fed might have to consider lowering interest rates sometime later in the year in order to stimulate growth.
The group of economists gave its economic forecast after meeting Tuesday with the members of the Federal Reserve Board.

Naroff stressed that the group's expectations for Fed policy were based strictly on the members' forecasts and not on what was said in the meeting. He also declined to say what was discussed in the meeting.
Overall, Naroff, who described Fed policy as being on a "knife's edge," said uncertainties in the forecast could make for some tough decisions for the central bank this year.
"The challenge in this environment is to determine the appropriate Fed policy when such minor variations in economic growth present such different outcomes for inflation and interest rates," he said.

While the bank economists' group said the chances were about even for either an interest-rate rise or cut in rates this year, it predicted no change in rates at the upcoming meeting of the Fed's policymaking arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, on Feb. 4-5.
